Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis

six weeks of arthritis, then joints and fever set the subtype · mimics · MAS and leukemia · uveitis screening · the treatment ladder

1Script2Urgent3Differential4Workup5Criteria6Severity7Treatment8Follow-upPractice
1Illness script
Bottom line
  • Arthritis for 6 weeks or more, starting before age 16, with no other cause is juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA), a clinical diagnosis; the first 6 months set the subtype: systemic (any joints plus daily fever spikes for 2 weeks or more), polyarticular (5 or more joints), oligoarticular (4 or fewer)
  • Treat with a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) first; methotrexate when arthritis persists; systemic JIA moves to an interleukin-1 (IL-1) or IL-6 blocker, with steroids only for refractory disease
  • Screen for silent uveitis with a slit lamp every 3 months in a young, antinuclear antibody (ANA) positive child; with two or more cell lines low in a child labeled systemic JIA, aspirate the bone marrow first
What it is

Chronic arthritis of childhood with no other cause, grouped into subtypes by the joint count and systemic features of the first 6 months

Systemic JIA (Still disease): arthritis with daily fever, rash, a big liver and spleen, nodes or serositis

Driver

Cause unknown: a genetic predisposition with autoimmune and autoinflammatory inflammation

Systemic JIA responds best to blocking IL-1 (anakinra) or IL-6 (tocilizumab)

Triggers

Oligoarticular: typically young girls, ages 2 to 4, the commonest subtype (non-modifiable)

Polyarticular: girls, peaks at 2 to 5 and 10 to 14 (non-modifiable)

Systemic: boys and girls equally, peak 2 to 4 (non-modifiable)

Enthesitis-related: older boys; HLA-B27 (human leukocyte antigen B27) more common (non-modifiable)

Chain

Joint: synovium inflamed swelling and stiffness on waking that eases through the day a limp or a joint not used

Systemic: daily fever spikes with a salmon rash anemia, high white count and platelets macrophage activation syndrome (MAS) in about 1 in 10

Eye: usually silent anterior uveitis (iridocyclitis) synechiae, cataract, glaucoma

Insights

Systemic JIA comes and goes; MAS does not. The fever spikes daily and the rash fades; in MAS the fever is unremitting, the rash constant, and the erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) falls ESRThe ESR depends on fibrinogen; MAS consumes fibrinogen, so the ESR drops even as inflammation peaks.

The uveitis gives no symptoms. It is usually silent, so a slit lamp on a schedule finds it, not a complaint

2Urgent risks
LeukemiaLabeled systemic JIA, now pale, petechiae, nodes, big liver and spleen

If two or more cell lines low, choose bone marrow aspiration before treating as JIA or MAS.

MASKnown systemic JIA, now unremitting fever, bleeding, a falling ESR

If ferritin up with platelets, fibrinogen and ESR falling, choose high-dose steroids; MAS kills through multiorgan failure. CriteriaIn a febrile child with systemic JIA: ferritin above 684 ng/mL plus any 2 of platelets 181,000/mm³ or less, AST above 48 units/L, triglycerides above 156 mg/dL, fibrinogen 360 mg/dL or less. Built for research; clinicians use them to support the diagnosis.

Septic jointOne hot joint in a child on methotrexate

If fever or one joint out of step with the rest, choose aspirate: septic until the fluid says otherwise.

3Differential
Daily fever with arthritis: most tempting first
DiagnosisFingerprintDecides it
Systemic JIA (Still disease)Evening fever spikes, salmon rash with each spike, big liver and spleenFever 2 weeks or more, arthritis 6 weeks or more; high WBC (white blood cell count), platelets and ferritin
Macrophage activation syndromeKnown systemic JIA; fever unremitting, rash constant, bleedingSudden; ferritin and triglycerides up, platelets, fibrinogen and ESR down
Acute lymphoblastic leukemia
Bone pain, nontender nodes, big liver and spleenTwo or more cell lines low; blasts in the bone marrow
Acute rheumatic fever
Migratory polyarthritis with carditisJones criteria: carditis, nodules, erythema marginatum, chorea
Systemic lupus erythematosusLupus lowers the countsAnemia, low white cells and platelets; systemic JIA raises them
Dengue or malariaAcute fever after travel to the tropicsDays; dengue: rash, low white cells and platelets; malaria: periodic fever, hemolytic anemia, blood smear
Swollen joints for weeks: most tempting first
DiagnosisFingerprintDecides it

4Workup
Clues that change the answer
CluePoints toNext move
Normal temperature in clinic; the log shows evening spikesSystemic JIATrust the log; continue the evaluation
Arthritis under 6 weeksNot JIA yetNSAID and reassess at 6 weeks
ESR falling as ferritin climbs in known systemic JIAMASHigh-dose steroids
Petechiae, pallor, nodes; two lines lowLeukemiaBone marrow aspiration
Adolescent girl, symmetric small joints, RF positiveRF-positive polyarticular JIAMethotrexate; a worse outlook
Older boy, enthesitis, HLA-B27
Enthesitis-related arthritisTeach the red, painful eye of acute uveitis

Pause point. The bait: a positive ANA read as lupus, or as proof against systemic JIA. ANA does not decide; the counts do: lupus lowers them, systemic JIA raises them.

5Diagnostic criteria
JIA subtypes Age – onset before 16 · Arthritis – 6 weeks or more, no other cause · Systemic – daily fever 2 weeks or more plus rash, nodes, big liver or spleen, or serositis; boys and girls equally · Polyarticular – 5 or more joints in the first 6 months; girls more · Oligoarticular – 4 or fewer joints in the first 6 months; typically young girls · Enthesitis-related – older boys; HLA-B27
6Severity
What sets the outcome
FindingMeansDo
Unremitting fever, bleeding, falling ESR in systemic JIAMAS: high mortality from multiorgan failureHigh-dose steroids
RF-positive polyarticular JIAA less favorable prognosisMethotrexate; a tumor necrosis factor (TNF) inhibitor if it fails
Uveitis foundSynechiae, cataract, glaucomaSteroid and dilating drops; methotrexate or anti-TNF if refractory
Long systemic steroid coursesGrowth retardation, osteoporosis, osteonecrosis (avascular necrosis)Inject the joint instead where possible
7Treatment
1

NSAIDany JIA, first

Naproxen; indomethacin in systemic JIA; may ease symptoms but does not change the course; no aspirin
2

Injecta few joints still swollen

Steroid injection into the joint, sparing systemic steroids
3

Methotrexatearthritis persists (oligo- or polyarticular)

Weekly methotrexate; check CBC, AST, alanine aminotransferase (ALT) and albumin
4

Biologicmethotrexate fails, or systemic JIA after NSAIDs

TNF inhibitor for oligo- or polyarticular; IL-1 (anakinra) or IL-6 (tocilizumab) blocker for systemic, where methotrexate and TNF inhibitors work poorly
5

Steroidsrefractory or severe systemic disease, or MAS

Systemic steroids, second line and not ideal in children; high-dose for MAS
8Follow-up
Follow-up decisions
WhenDo
Oligo- or RF-negative polyarticular, ANA positive, under 7 at onset, within 4 yearsSlit-lamp exam every 3 months ACR 2019High risk, every 3 months: oligoarthritis, RF-negative polyarthritis, psoriatic or undifferentiated arthritis that is also ANA positive, under 7 at onset and within 4 years of onset. Everyone else (ANA negative, 7 or older at onset, past 4 years, systemic JIA, RF-positive polyarthritis, enthesitis-related arthritis): every 6 to 12 months. A simpler rule: every 3 months if ANA positive, every 6 if negative.
Other subtypes, ANA negative, 7 or older at onset, or past 4 yearsSlit-lamp exam every 6 to 12 months
Systemic JIAEye exam once or twice a year
On methotrexateCBC, AST, ALT and albumin; one hot joint is septic until the fluid says otherwise
Practice
  1. 5-year-old girl with 6 weeks of swollen knees and wrists 3 weeks of fever to 39.5 °C each evening, normal by morning salmon-pink rash with each spike that fades hepatosplenomegaly WBC 21,000/mm³ · platelets 610,000/mm³ · ANA low-titer positive · RF negative → Systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis → quotidian fever with an evanescent rash and 6 weeks of arthritis, with high counts: systemic JIA; a low-titer ANA does not exclude it, lupus lowers counts, and rheumatic fever's joints migrate, with carditis or erythema marginatum
  2. 5-year-old girl with 2 weeks of daily fever and 3 weeks of a swollen right knee parents' log: spikes to 39.8 °C each evening rash with each spike Seen in the afternoon, well appearing T 37.0 °C · ESR 64 mm/h → Continue the evaluation for systemic JIA → quotidian fever returns to normal between spikes, so a normal clinic temperature excludes nothing; no focus and well between spikes is not a bacterial infection
  3. 6-year-old boy diagnosed with systemic JIA a year ago, now persistently febrile oozing at venipuncture sites hepatosplenomegaly WBC 6,000/mm³ · platelets 92,000/mm³ · ferritin 18,000 ng/mL · fibrinogen 110 mg/dL · ESR 6 mm/h (70 last month) · AST 220 U/L · triglycerides 380 mg/dL → Macrophage activation syndrome → in systemic JIA, persistent fever with ESR and fibrinogen falling as ferritin, triglycerides and AST climb, and oozing from consumed clotting factors: macrophage activation syndrome; with only platelets low, high-dose steroids
  4. 4-year-old girl diagnosed 1 month ago with arthritis of the left knee and right ankle ANA positive no eye pain, redness or blurred vision Knee swelling improving on naproxen Afebrile · visual acuity 20/30 both eyes → Slit-lamp exam for asymptomatic uveitis → young, ANA positive and few joints carries the highest uveitis risk, and it is silent: slit-lamp exams every 3 months
  5. 4-year-old boy with 6 weeks of evening fever spikes since a trip to Costa Rica pink rash with each spike, gone by morning right knee swollen 6 weeks; spleen tip palpable Well between spikes hemoglobin 10.4 g/dL · platelets 640,000/mm³ → Systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis → weeks of quotidian fever with an evanescent rash, mild anemia and high platelets: systemic JIA; dengue lasts days and lowers the white cells and platelets, and malaria brings periodic fever with hemolytic anemia, seen on a blood smear
  6. 7-year-old boy with 4 weeks of daily evening fevers to 39.6 °C normal temperature each morning salmon rash during fevers; both knees and the left wrist swollen for 7 weeks pericardial rub Afebrile in clinic → High WBC and platelets, high ferritin; ANA and RF negative → systemic JIA is inflammation without autoantibodies: high WBC, platelets, ESR and ferritin; ANA and RF usually negative
  7. 3-year-old girl with 8 weeks of a swollen, warm left knee limps after waking, better by afternoon right ankle also swollen No fever or rash; lives in a nonendemic area; no tick bites Afebrile · ANA positive → Oligoarticular juvenile idiopathic arthritis → 4 or fewer joints for 8 weeks with morning stiffness: oligoarticular JIA; nonendemic with no tick bite argues against Lyme; ANA positive and young: slit-lamp exams
  8. 13-year-old girl with 2 months of aching legs, hips and back pain the same all day; no morning stiffness no joint swelling; tibias tender to pressure Strict vegan diet without fortified foods Afebrile · height and weight steady → Vitamin D deficiency → diffuse bone pain that never eases and no swollen joints, on an unfortified vegan diet: vitamin D and calcium
  9. 14-year-old girl, ankles aching 3 months since starting daily walks this month knees, elbows, wrists; all swollen bilaterally stiff mornings that ease Tired despite 9 hours' sleep; new plant-based diet Afebrile · weight 95th to 90th percentile · height steady · chest normal → Naproxen → 5 or more joints within months, symmetric, stiff in the morning and easing: polyarticular JIA; naproxen first, methotrexate if it persists; deficiency pain never eases or swells joints, and falling weight with steady height is not hypothyroidism
  10. 4-year-old girl labeled systemic JIA 6 weeks ago, joints improving on naproxen now pale, with petechiae on her trunk and legs lymph nodes enlarged in the neck and groin T 39.4 °C · hemoglobin 8.1 g/dL · WBC 2,100/mm³ · platelets 38,000/mm³ → Bone marrow aspiration → low counts in two or more cell lines in a child labeled systemic JIA: bone marrow first; leukemia mimics JIA with bone pain, nodes and a big liver and spleen
  11. 9-year-old boy with 3 weeks of a swollen right knee stiff after waking, better by noon no preceding diarrhea, urethritis or rash; nonendemic area No injury; walks with a slight limp Afebrile · WBC normal · ESR 32 mm/h → Naproxen and reassess at 6 weeks → JIA needs 6 weeks of arthritis with no other cause: treat the pain and reassess before labeling it or starting methotrexate
Pairs with Acute Leukemia in a Child: the marrow comes before the steroid. Septic Arthritis in a Child: one hot joint on methotrexate. The Limping Child: sick or well, then age and time.
Transferable rule

Before naming JIA, time the arthritis, chart the fever and look at every cell line.
